summary: Defines Session Traversal Utilities for NAT, a tool other protocols use to deal with NAT. An endpoint can learn the IP address and port a NAT gave it, check connectivity between two endpoints, and keep NAT bindings alive.

plainLanguage.summary: Behind a home router, a device does not know its outside address. STUN is a friend outside who tells you what address they see.

subtitle: A small toolkit that lets a device behind a NAT learn its public address and keep its NAT bindings alive.

tldr.problem: A host behind one or more NATs does not know which public IP address and port the NAT gave it, so it cannot tell a peer where to send traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends a Binding request to a STUN server on the public Internet. The server copies the request's source transport address into an XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS attribute in its response. The message has a 20-byte header followed by TLV attributes.
tldr.outcome: STUN is not a complete NAT traversal solution. It is a tool used inside larger solutions called STUN Usages, such as ICE. RFC 8489 obsoletes RFC 5389.

today: RFC 8489 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2020. It obsoletes RFC 5389 and, per the unit metadata, has not itself been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: A Tool for Dealing with NATs
sections.content:
Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN) gives an endpoint a way to learn the IP address and port that a Network Address Translator (NAT) allocated for its private address and port. It can also keep a NAT binding alive. With some extensions it can check connectivity between two endpoints or relay packets between them.

The RFC is explicit that STUN is not a NAT traversal solution by itself. It is a tool used inside a solution. Each such solution is called a STUN Usage, and it decides when messages are sent, which optional attributes are included, which server is used and which authentication is applied. Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) is one usage and SIP Outbound is another.

RFC 8489 obsoletes RFC 5389. It defines an extensible packet format, operation over several transports, and two forms of authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: STUN is like asking a friend across the street what your house number looks like from where they stand. It is one handy trick, not the whole plan for getting visitors to your door.

sections.title: How a Binding Exchange Works
sections.content:
STUN is a client-server protocol with two kinds of transaction. In a request/response transaction the client sends a request and the server answers. In an indication transaction either side sends a message that gets no response. Both carry a randomly chosen 96-bit transaction ID.

This document defines one method, Binding. When a Binding request crosses a NAT, the NAT rewrites the source transport address. The server sees the public address created by the NAT closest to it, called the reflexive transport address, and copies it into an XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS attribute in the success response. The NAT rewrites only the IP header on the way back, so the address in the body reaches the client untouched.

Binding can also be sent as an indication. The mere receipt of an indication refreshes the bindings in the NATs on the path, which makes it a keep-alive.
sections.plainLanguage: You send a letter to a friend. They read the return address on the envelope, which the post office stamped for you, and write it back to you. Now you know the address the outside world sees.

sections.title: The STUN Message and Its Attributes
sections.content:
Every STUN message has a 20-byte header followed by zero or more attributes. The header holds a message type, a message length, a magic cookie and the transaction ID. The two most significant bits are always zero. The message type packs a 12-bit method and a 2-bit class (request, indication, success response or error response). The magic cookie is always 0x2112A442. The length counts the message without the 20-byte header and, because attributes are padded, its last two bits are always zero. These fixed values help tell STUN from other protocols sharing a port.

Each attribute is Type-Length-Value (TLV) encoded with a 16-bit type and a 16-bit length, and ends on a 32-bit boundary, padded with 1, 2 or 3 zero bytes. Types from 0x0000 to 0x7FFF are comprehension-required: an agent that does not understand one cannot process the message. Types from 0x8000 to 0xFFFF are comprehension-optional and can be ignored.

XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS holds the reflexive address XORed with the magic cookie (and, for IPv6, also the transaction ID). The plain MAPPED-ADDRESS is kept only for backwards compatibility, because some NATs were found rewriting the address bytes they spotted in payloads.

Other attributes include USERNAME, MESSAGE-INTEGRITY, MESSAGE-INTEGRITY-SHA256, ERROR-CODE, UNKNOWN-ATTRIBUTES, SOFTWARE and FINGERPRINT. The FINGERPRINT value is a CRC-32 XORed with 0x5354554e and must be the last attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message starts with a fixed label saying what kind of note it is, then adds extra labeled slips. Slips you do not understand can be skipped only if they are marked optional.

sections.title: Sending, Retrying and Receiving
sections.content:
STUN can run over UDP, TCP, TLS-over-TCP or DTLS-over-UDP. Over UDP the client itself retransmits a request, starting at an interval called the RTO and doubling it each time. The initial RTO SHOULD be at least 500 ms. The default is a total of 7 requests (Rc), and the client gives up once 16 times the RTO (Rm) passes after the last one. With an RTO of 500 ms the example times are 0, 500, 1500, 3500, 7500, 15500 and 31500 ms, and failure is declared at 39500 ms. Indications are never retransmitted. A client SHOULD limit itself to ten outstanding transactions to one server.

Over TCP, retransmission is left to TCP, and the default timeout is 39.5 seconds. A server MUST NOT ever open a connection back toward the client to send a response.

A receiver first checks the basics: the first two bits are zero, the magic cookie is correct, the length is sensible, and the method and class are allowed. Bad messages are silently discarded. A request with an unknown comprehension-required attribute gets error 420 with an UNKNOWN-ATTRIBUTES attribute. The Binding method is idempotent, so a server can recompute a response for a retransmitted request instead of storing state.

Clients find servers through DNS. A stun or stuns URI is resolved with SRV records, falling back to A and AAAA lookups. The default port is 3478 for UDP and TCP, and 5349 for TLS and DTLS.
sections.plainLanguage: If you do not hear back, you ask again, waiting a bit longer each time, and eventually you stop asking. Some notes need no answer at all, like a quick wave to say you are still there.

sections.title: Credentials and Message Integrity
sections.content:
Authentication is optional, and each usage says whether to use it. There are two mechanisms. Both prove integrity with an HMAC over the message, using MESSAGE-INTEGRITY (HMAC-SHA1, 20 bytes) or MESSAGE-INTEGRITY-SHA256 (HMAC-SHA256, up to 32 bytes).

The short-term credential mechanism assumes the client and server already exchanged a time-limited username and password through another channel, as ICE does by signaling. There is no challenge.

The long-term credential mechanism uses a provisioned username and password and a digest challenge. The client first sends a request with no credentials. The server rejects it with error 401 and gives a REALM and a NONCE. The client retries with its username, the realm, the nonce and a message-integrity value. If the nonce has expired, the server answers 438 (Stale Nonce) with a fresh one. Long-term credentials cannot protect indications, because indications cannot be challenged.

New in this version are a PASSWORD-ALGORITHMS list (MD5 or SHA-256) and a USERHASH attribute that hides the username. To stop an attacker from stripping these features, the server prefixes the nonce with obMatJos2 and bits that record which security features are in use.
sections.plainLanguage: Two friends can agree on a secret handshake first. Or a guard can ask for a password, hand you a one-time ticket number, and check both when you come back.

sections.title: Attacks and Defenses
sections.content:
Message integrity defeats an outsider who modifies messages in transit or races in a fake error response. Some authentication errors cannot be protected, and running STUN inside TLS or DTLS mitigates those cases. The HMAC approach is open to offline dictionary attacks, so strong passwords are advised. The RFC also notes that SHA-256 is fast and does not meet modern standards for slowing down password searches. It was chosen for consistency with RFC 7616.

A rogue client could use a STUN server as a reflector by faking its source address. There is no amplification in the number of packets, and ingress source address filtering mitigates it. Revealing the SOFTWARE value may help attackers, so implementers SHOULD make it configurable.

The more serious attacks target the usage. An on-path attacker can change the source address of a Binding request so the client learns a false reflexive address. This can be used to aim traffic at a victim, to silence a client, to impersonate a client or to eavesdrop. A message-integrity value cannot cover the source IP address, so the RFC points to the approach in ICE, where the client verifies the learned address.
sections.plainLanguage: A trickster in the middle could tell you the wrong return address so your mail goes to the wrong place. Checking the address another way, and sending your mail in a locked pouch, helps.

sections.title: Registries and What Changed
sections.content:
IANA keeps registries for STUN methods, attributes, error codes, password algorithms and security features. The security features registry has 24 bits, with bit 0 for password algorithms and bit 1 for username anonymity. Method 0x001 is Binding. The registered ports are 3478 (TCP and UDP) and 5349 (TCP, for stuns).

Compared with RFC 5389, this version adds DTLS-over-UDP support, STUN URIs, SHA-256 message integrity, a choice of password algorithm, anonymous usernames, bid-down protection, an alternate-domain option for redirection, and a test vector. It also no longer permits sharing a NONCE across different source addresses or ports.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a public list of every kind of note, slip and error number, so everyone uses the same ones. This new edition added a few new kinds of slip.

fields.desc: The most significant 2 bits MUST be zeroes.

fields.desc: Size in bytes, not counting the 20-byte header.

fields.desc: Cryptographically random identifier chosen by the sender.

items.desc: The NONCE is no longer valid; retry with the new one.
